authoredFrom: PS8 (a suppression filter must not eat a real declaration) + PS10 (every parameter form must be read). Authored 2026-09-26. PS8 has TWO halves and both were measured. (a) The pre-wave `AUTOMATIC_VARIABLES` set carried `foreach` and `switch` — LANGUAGE KEYWORDS, not automatic variables; reproduced as 6 of 9 top-level assignments silently dropped. (b) Every suppression compared CASE-SENSITIVELY while PowerShell identifiers are case-insensitive: measured on `ansible@7ec731b`, `exec_wrapper.ps1` published `null` as a variable FIVE times, and `$Script:AnsibleClrFacadeSet` was published as a variable named `Script:AnsibleClrFacadeSet`. The ledger's standing rule names this class — "every language's fixtures MUST include identifiers that collide with stdlib/builtin words, because suppression filters are invisible to output-diff tests otherwise" — and this lane had no fixtures, so nothing pinned it. PS10: `function G($x, $y)` published ZERO parameters. The grammar's real shape, measured, is `function_statement > function_parameter_declaration > parameter_list > script_parameter` — the wrapper is named `function_parameter_declaration` and the ITEMS are `script_parameter`; a first fix that assumed the items were the wrapper matched nothing and the fixture caught it.

expectParameters.comment: PS10, the INLINE form — the row the mutant powershell/drop-inline-parameters found missing. It transformed the result correctly and the suite did not notice, because nothing asserted this symbol's parameters: the suppression fixture pinned the SYMBOL and payload-psb11 pinned only Get-Report. A mutant that fires and changes nothing is a coverage gap the mutant found, which is the whole reason the lane needed one.
